title: Ezekiel 45:9–17
context: The Lord GOD addresses the princes of Israel directly: enough violence and plunder; execute justice and righteousness, and stop dispossessing his people. He requires just balances and standard measures for the ephah, the bath, the homer, the shekel, and the mina, echoing the law’s demand for honest weights (Leviticus 19:35–36; Deuteronomy 25:15; compare Proverbs 11:1; Amos 8:5; Micah 6:11). The people are to give set portions of grain, oil, and sheep as an offering for the prince, and the prince is to provide the burnt offerings, meal offerings, drink offerings, sin offerings, and peace offerings for the feasts, new moons, and Sabbaths, to make atonement for the house of Israel. The prince is presented as the responsible provider for public worship, and his identity is best held with care (compare 34:24; 37:25). The question of sacrifices in this vision is treated at 40:38–49 and 44:15–31. Readers in both traditions take the temple vision of chapters 40–48 in the ways named at 40:1–16. Arminian and Reformed readers generally treat the call to justice and honest dealing as shared ground.

verses.text: “ ‘The Lord GOD says: “Enough, you princes of Israel! Remove violence and plunder, and execute justice and righteousness! Stop dispossessing my people!” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Lord GOD telling the princes to stop violence and plunder and to execute justice and righteousness. Rulers must stop dispossessing the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s direct rebuke of oppressive rulers. Both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground about God’s demand for justice from those in power.

verses.text: “You shall have just balances, a just ephah, and a just bath.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the command to have just balances and measures. Honesty in trade is part of faithfulness to God in daily life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the echo of Leviticus 19:36 and Proverbs 11:1. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about integrity in everyday dealings.

verses.text: The ephah and the bath shall be of one measure, that the bath may contain one tenth of a homer, and the ephah one tenth of a homer. Its measure shall be the same as the homer.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the ephah and bath set to a common standard. Fair measures protect ordinary people from being cheated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see standardization serving justice. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the wider call to honest measures.

verses.text: The shekel shall be twenty gerahs. Twenty shekels plus twenty-five shekels plus fifteen shekels shall be your mina.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the shekel and mina defined by fixed standards. Clear standards prevent the powerful from abusing the weak.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see detailed regulation of weights as an expression of God’s concern for fairness (compare Micah 6:11). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse within that call to justice.

verses.text: “ ‘ “This is the offering that you shall offer: the sixth part of an ephah from a homer of wheat, and you shall give the sixth part of an ephah from a homer of barley,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a set portion of wheat and barley given as an offering. Worship involves real and proportionate giving.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see proportionate offerings required of the people. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the vision’s ordered provision for worship.

verses.text: and the set portion of oil, of the bath of oil, one tenth of a bath out of the cor, which is ten baths, even a homer (for ten baths are a homer),
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a set portion of oil given according to standard measures. Offerings are measured fairly for everyone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same concern for honest measures applied to worship. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse within the larger provision for offerings.

verses.text: and one lamb of the flock out of two hundred, from the well-watered pastures of Israel—for a meal offering, for a burnt offering, and for peace offerings, to make atonement for them,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a lamb from the flock given for offerings to make atonement. Readers hold several views of such offerings in light of Hebrews 10.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the language of atonement and note the question raised by Hebrews 10:4, 12. Both traditions commonly hold the main readings of these sacrifices with care, without declaring a winner.

verses.text: “All the people of the land shall give to this offering for the prince in Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see all the people of the land contributing to the offering for the prince. Worship is a shared responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the whole community participating in public worship through the prince. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the vision’s ordered life.

verses.text: It shall be the prince’s part to give the burnt offerings, the meal offerings, and the drink offerings, in the feasts, and on the new moons, and on the Sabbaths, in all the appointed feasts of the house of Israel. He shall prepare the sin offering, the meal offering, the burnt offering, and the peace offerings, to make atonement for the house of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the prince providing offerings for the feasts, new moons, and Sabbaths, including sin offerings to make atonement. His role is to serve the people’s worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prince as provider rather than priest, and hold the sacrifice question in light of Hebrews 10:12. Both traditions commonly hold the prince’s identity and the offerings’ meaning with care.
